title: Spinal Cord Injury
description: Acute spinal cord injury care, including immobilization, airway management in cervical injuries, spinal versus neurogenic shock, autonomic dysreflexia, halo vest care, bowel and bladder programs, complication prevention, and rehabilitation.
keyPoints: Assume a spinal injury after trauma: keep the spine in neutral alignment with a cervical collar and backboard, and log roll with at least 3 people.

Injuries at C3-C5 threaten the phrenic nerve and diaphragm ("C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive"). Watch vital capacity, RR, SpO2, ABGs, and cough strength. Injuries above C3 usually need a ventilator.
Spinal shock: temporary loss of all reflexes, sensation, and motor function below the injury (flaccid paralysis). Its end is signaled by returning reflexes and spasticity.
Neurogenic shock (injury at T6 or above): loss of sympathetic tone causes hypotension, bradycardia, and warm, dry skin. Treat with IV fluids, vasopressors, and atropine.

Autonomic dysreflexia (T6 and above): severe hypertension, pounding headache, bradycardia, flushing and sweating above the injury. Sit the client upright, loosen clothing, find and remove the cause (bladder first, then bowel, then skin), and notify the provider.
Complete injury: no motor or sensory function below the level. Incomplete injury: some function preserved, including sacral sparing, with a better prognosis.
Halo vest: keep the wrench taped to the vest, never lift or turn the client by the halo, do pin-site care, and check skin under the vest.

Prevent complications: bowel program at a consistent time, intermittent catheterization, turning and pressure relief, DVT prophylaxis (SCDs, LMWH), and psychosocial support through grieving and rehab.

questions.stem: A client is admitted after a motorcycle crash with a suspected cervical spine injury and is wearing a cervical collar. The nurse needs to turn the client to inspect the back. Which approach is correct?

options.text: Remove the collar briefly so the client can turn their own head and shoulders
options.rationale: The collar must stay in place until the spine is cleared. Removing it and letting the client move could worsen a cord injury.

options.text: Log roll with three or more staff, one keeping the head in line with the body
options.rationale: Log rolling with one person dedicated to the head keeps the head, neck, and trunk aligned as one unit and prevents secondary cord injury.

options.text: Have the client grasp the side rail and pull to turn toward it while the nurse supports the hips and legs
options.rationale: Pulling on the rail twists the spine and can displace an unstable fracture.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed to 45° before turning to make the client more comfortable
options.rationale: Flexing the spine by raising the head of the bed is not done with an uncleared spine unless the provider orders it, such as reverse Trendelenburg.

questions.explanation: Until imaging clears the spine, any trauma client is treated as having an unstable spinal injury. Maintain neutral alignment with a collar and firm support, and log roll with a team (one person controls the head) to prevent further damage to the cord.

questions.stem: A client with an acute C4 spinal cord injury is admitted to the ICU. Which assessment finding is most important for the nurse to report immediately?

options.text: Absence of sensation below the shoulders
options.rationale: Loss of sensation below the injury is expected with a C4 injury and is not a new emergency.

options.text: Flaccid paralysis of all four extremities with absent deep tendon reflexes throughout
options.rationale: Flaccid quadriplegia with absent reflexes is expected during spinal shock with a cervical injury.

options.text: Temperature of 99.1°F (37.3°C)
options.rationale: This is a minimal elevation that warrants monitoring but does not threaten life.

options.text: Vital capacity that has dropped from 1.8 L to 1.0 L with a weak cough
options.rationale: C3-C5 injuries affect the phrenic nerve. Falling vital capacity and a weak cough signal impending respiratory failure, which may need intubation. Ascending cord edema can make breathing worse in the first days.

questions.explanation: The phrenic nerve (C3-C5) controls the diaphragm. With high cervical injuries, airway and breathing are the priority. Monitor RR, depth, SpO2, ABGs, vital capacity, and cough strength, because cord edema can extend upward during the first 24-72 hours.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client with a C5 spinal cord injury. Which findings indicate the client may be developing respiratory failure? Select all that apply.

options.text: PaCO2 rising from 40 to 52 mm Hg
options.rationale: Rising CO2 shows hypoventilation as the respiratory muscles fatigue or the diaphragm weakens.

options.text: Rapid, shallow respirations at 32/min
options.rationale: Tachypnea with shallow breaths is a compensatory sign of respiratory muscle weakness.

options.text: Inability to cough up secretions effectively
options.rationale: Loss of abdominal and intercostal muscle function weakens the cough, causing retained secretions, atelectasis, and pneumonia.

options.text: SpO2 98% on 2 L nasal cannula
options.rationale: This oxygenation is adequate. SpO2 can also remain normal on oxygen even while CO2 is rising, so it is not a sensitive early sign.

options.text: Declining vital capacity on serial measurements
options.rationale: A trending decline in vital capacity is one of the earliest objective signs of respiratory failure in SCI.

options.text: Heart rate of 54/min with warm, dry skin
options.rationale: Bradycardia with warm, dry skin points to neurogenic shock, not respiratory failure.

questions.explanation: Cervical injuries weaken the diaphragm, intercostal, and abdominal muscles. Early signs of respiratory failure include falling vital capacity, rising PaCO2, rapid shallow breathing, a weak cough, and fatigue. Interventions include assisted (quad) coughing, suctioning, incentive spirometry, and early intubation when needed.

questions.stem: A nursing student asks how spinal shock differs from neurogenic shock. Which explanation by the nurse is most accurate?

options.text: "Spinal shock is a temporary loss of reflexes below the injury. Neurogenic shock is hypotension and bradycardia from lost sympathetic tone."
options.rationale: Spinal shock is a neurologic phenomenon (flaccid paralysis, areflexia). Neurogenic shock is a hemodynamic one caused by loss of sympathetic outflow, usually with injuries at T6 or above.

options.text: "They are two names for the same condition."
options.rationale: They are distinct. They can occur together, but one involves reflexes and the other circulation.

options.text: "Spinal shock causes hypertension, while neurogenic shock causes hypotension."
options.rationale: Spinal shock does not cause hypertension. Hypertension in SCI suggests autonomic dysreflexia, which occurs after spinal shock resolves.

options.text: "Neurogenic shock is caused by blood loss from the injury site, while spinal shock is the temporary loss of reflexes and movement below the level of injury."
options.rationale: The description of spinal shock is right, but shock from blood loss is hypovolemic shock. Neurogenic shock is a distributive shock caused by vasodilation from lost sympathetic tone.

questions.explanation: Spinal shock is a temporary loss of all reflexes, sensation, and motor function below the injury, lasting days to weeks. Returning reflexes signal its end. Neurogenic shock results from loss of sympathetic tone and produces hypotension, bradycardia, and warm, dry skin from vasodilation.

questions.stem: A client with a T2 spinal cord injury from a fall 4 hours ago has BP 80/46 mm Hg, HR 48/min, and warm, dry, pink skin below the injury. There is no evidence of bleeding. Which treatment should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Furosemide IV and fluid restriction
options.rationale: Diuresis would worsen hypotension. This client needs volume and vascular support, not fluid removal.

options.text: Rapid transfusion of packed red blood cells using the massive transfusion protocol
options.rationale: There is no evidence of hemorrhage. Bradycardia with warm skin points away from hypovolemic shock, which causes tachycardia and cool skin.

options.text: IV fluids, vasopressors, and atropine for symptomatic bradycardia
options.rationale: These are signs of neurogenic shock. Loss of sympathetic tone causes vasodilation and unopposed vagal activity. Treatment restores vascular tone and heart rate.

options.text: Nifedipine to correct autonomic dysreflexia
options.rationale: Autonomic dysreflexia causes severe hypertension, not hypotension, and usually appears after spinal shock resolves.

questions.explanation: Neurogenic shock (injury at T6 or above) produces the triad of hypotension, bradycardia, and warm, dry skin. Unlike hypovolemic or cardiogenic shock, the heart rate is slow and the skin is warm. Treatment includes IV fluids, vasopressors (such as norepinephrine), atropine for bradycardia, and keeping mean arterial pressure high enough to perfuse the cord.

questions.stem: A client with a T4 spinal cord injury suddenly reports a pounding headache and blurred vision. BP is 210/110 mm Hg (baseline 104/62), HR is 50/min, and the face is flushed and sweaty. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Lower the head of the bed and elevate the legs
options.rationale: Lying flat increases blood pressure further. This is the opposite of what is needed.

options.text: Sit the client upright with the legs lowered
options.rationale: Sitting upright with the legs down pools blood in the lower extremities and lowers BP quickly. It is the first action for autonomic dysreflexia.

options.text: Give the scheduled dose of baclofen
options.rationale: Baclofen treats spasticity and does not address the hypertensive emergency or its cause.

options.text: Leave the room to call the provider before doing anything else
options.rationale: The nurse should stay with the client and act immediately. Notifying the provider happens alongside assessment, not instead of first actions.

questions.explanation: Autonomic dysreflexia is a hypertensive emergency in clients with injuries at T6 or above. A noxious stimulus below the injury triggers massive sympathetic discharge. Sit the client up immediately, loosen tight clothing, check BP every 2-5 minutes, and find and remove the trigger.

questions.stem: A client with a C6 spinal cord injury develops autonomic dysreflexia with BP 198/108 mm Hg. Place the nurse's actions in the correct order.

items.text: Sit the client upright with the legs lowered
Loosen tight clothing, abdominal binders, and leg-bag straps
Check the urinary catheter for kinks and the bladder for distention, and drain the bladder
Check the rectum for fecal impaction using anesthetic lubricant
Notify the provider for an antihypertensive if BP stays elevated after the cause is removed

questions.explanation: First lower BP by positioning upright, then remove constricting items. Next, search for the trigger: the bladder is the most common cause (distention or a kinked catheter), followed by the bowel (impaction). Use anesthetic lubricant to avoid making the stimulus worse. BP is rechecked every 2-5 minutes throughout. If BP stays high, the provider may order a fast-acting antihypertensive such as nifedipine or nitroglycerin.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching the family of a client with a T3 spinal cord injury about common triggers of autonomic dysreflexia. Which triggers should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Full bladder or kinked catheter tubing
options.rationale: Bladder distention is the most common trigger of autonomic dysreflexia.

options.text: Constipation or fecal impaction
options.rationale: A distended bowel is the second most common trigger.

options.text: Pressure injury or ingrown toenail
options.rationale: Painful skin stimuli below the injury can trigger the reflex even though the client cannot feel them.

options.text: Tight clothing or shoes
options.rationale: Constriction below the level of injury is a noxious stimulus that can trigger an episode.

options.text: Sitting upright in a wheelchair
options.rationale: Sitting upright does not trigger dysreflexia. It is the first intervention used to lower BP during an episode.

options.text: Drinking a glass of water
options.rationale: Normal fluid intake is not a trigger. Adequate fluids are part of bowel and bladder programs.

questions.explanation: Any noxious stimulus below the level of injury can trigger autonomic dysreflexia in clients injured at T6 or above. Bladder causes are most common, then bowel, then skin (pressure injuries, tight clothing, burns, ingrown nails). Prevention depends on consistent bowel and bladder programs and skin care.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing a rehabilitation unit's client list. Which client is at greatest risk for autonomic dysreflexia?

options.text: A client with a complete T4 injury 3 months ago
options.rationale: Autonomic dysreflexia occurs with injuries at T6 or above and typically appears after spinal shock has resolved, making this client at highest risk.

options.text: A client with an L2 injury 3 months ago
options.rationale: Lumbar injuries are below T6, so sympathetic outflow is largely preserved and dysreflexia is not expected.

options.text: A client with a T10 injury 6 months ago
options.rationale: T10 is below the major splanchnic outflow, so the risk of autonomic dysreflexia is low.

options.text: A client with a sacral injury 1 year ago
options.rationale: Sacral injuries do not interrupt the sympathetic regulation that causes autonomic dysreflexia.

questions.explanation: Autonomic dysreflexia requires an injury at or above T6, above the major splanchnic sympathetic outflow. It usually appears once spinal shock resolves and reflex activity returns, and it can recur throughout the client's life.

questions.stem: A client's spinal cord injury is described as "incomplete." Which finding is consistent with an incomplete injury?

options.text: Total loss of motor function and sensation below the level of injury
options.rationale: This describes a complete injury.

options.text: Absent reflexes in the first days after injury
options.rationale: Areflexia early after injury reflects spinal shock and can occur with both complete and incomplete injuries.

options.text: Hypotension and bradycardia
options.rationale: These are signs of neurogenic shock and do not show whether the injury is complete or incomplete.

options.text: Preserved perianal sensation and some voluntary toe movement
options.rationale: Any preserved motor or sensory function below the injury, especially sacral sparing, indicates an incomplete injury and a better potential for recovery.

questions.explanation: A complete injury has no motor or sensory function below the injury level. An incomplete injury preserves some function, such as sacral sparing, and includes patterns like central cord, Brown-Séquard, and anterior cord syndromes. Incomplete injuries have a better prognosis for recovery.

questions.stem: A client with a cervical fracture is placed in a halo vest. Which action by the nurse is correct?

options.text: Use the halo ring as a handle to help the client sit up
options.rationale: Lifting or turning the client by the halo ring or bars can loosen pins and displace the fracture.

options.text: Tighten any loose pins with the wrench that is kept attached to the vest
options.rationale: Only the provider adjusts pins. A loose pin is reported, not adjusted by the nurse.

options.text: Keep the wrench taped to the front of the vest at all times
options.rationale: The wrench must stay with the vest so the anterior panel can be removed quickly for CPR or another emergency.

options.text: Remove the vest every shift to bathe the skin underneath
options.rationale: The vest is not removed for routine care because that would destabilize the cervical spine. Skin is cleaned by reaching under the liner.

questions.explanation: Halo vest care: keep the wrench attached for emergencies, never lift or move the client by the halo, do pin-site care per protocol, assess for infection and loose pins, check the skin under the vest for pressure, and monitor neuro status.

questions.stem: A client is being discharged home in a halo vest. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Clean the pin sites as instructed and report redness, drainage, or increasing pain
options.rationale: Pin sites are a portal for infection, including osteomyelitis. Signs of infection must be reported.

options.text: Report a pin that feels loose or a clicking sound
options.rationale: A loose pin can compromise stability and must be evaluated by the provider.

options.text: Turn your whole body, not just your head, to look to the side
options.rationale: The halo prevents neck movement, so the client must turn the whole body. Mirrors help the client see around them.

options.text: You may drive as long as you use your mirrors
options.rationale: Driving is unsafe because peripheral vision and the ability to turn the head are severely limited.

options.text: Check the skin under the vest edges for redness or breakdown
options.rationale: The vest and liner can cause pressure injuries, especially over bony prominences.

options.text: Have a family member lift you by the bars when you get out of bed
options.rationale: The halo frame is never used to lift or reposition the client because it can loosen pins and disrupt alignment.

questions.explanation: Halo vest teaching covers pin-site care and signs of infection, reporting loose pins, skin checks under the vest, turning the whole body, no driving, and never using the frame to lift. The client and family should also know where the wrench is kept for emergencies.

questions.stem: The nurse is establishing a bowel program for a client with a T8 spinal cord injury. Which intervention is most appropriate?

options.text: Give a suppository with digital stimulation at the same time daily, about 30 minutes after a meal
options.rationale: A consistent schedule timed to the gastrocolic reflex after a meal, with suppository and digital stimulation, promotes predictable evacuation and prevents incontinence and impaction.

options.text: Give an oral stimulant laxative whenever the client has not had a bowel movement for 3 to 4 days
options.rationale: Waiting days and using laxatives as needed leads to impaction and unpredictable incontinence. A bowel program relies on routine.

options.text: Restrict fluids to 1,000 mL/day to prevent bowel incontinence
options.rationale: Restricting fluids causes hard stools and constipation. The client needs adequate fluids, unless restricted for another reason, plus fiber.

options.text: Schedule bowel care at a different time each day to match therapy sessions
options.rationale: Varying the time defeats the purpose of conditioning the bowel to empty predictably.

questions.explanation: Bowel programs for SCI use a consistent daily or every-other-day time (often after a meal to use the gastrocolic reflex), a suppository or mini-enema, digital stimulation, high fiber, and adequate fluids. A regular program prevents impaction, which is also a trigger for autonomic dysreflexia.

questions.stem: The nurse has taught a client with a T10 spinal cord injury how to perform intermittent self-catheterization. Which statement by the client indicates correct understanding?

options.text: "I only need to catheterize when I feel that my bladder is full."
options.rationale: Clients with SCI usually cannot feel bladder fullness. Waiting for the sensation leads to overdistention and urinary tract infections.

options.text: "I'll limit my fluids to a few sips a day so that I don't have to catheterize as often."
options.rationale: Severe fluid restriction concentrates urine and increases the risk of UTI and urinary stones.

options.text: "Cloudy, foul-smelling urine is normal with catheterization."
options.rationale: Cloudy, foul-smelling urine suggests a UTI and should be reported.

options.text: "I'll catheterize on a schedule, about every 4 to 6 hours, even if I don't feel full."
options.rationale: Scheduled catheterization (often every 4-6 hours, keeping volumes under about 500 mL) prevents overdistention, reflux, and infection.

questions.explanation: Neurogenic bladder after SCI is managed with scheduled intermittent catheterization, adequate fluids, and monitoring for UTI. Keeping the bladder from overdistending also prevents autonomic dysreflexia in clients with higher injuries.

questions.stem: The nurse is planning care to prevent complications for a client with a new T6 complete spinal cord injury. Which interventions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Apply sequential compression devices and give enoxaparin as prescribed
options.rationale: Immobility and loss of vasomotor tone put SCI clients at very high risk for DVT and PE, so mechanical and pharmacologic prophylaxis are standard.

options.text: Reposition the client at least every 2 hours and inspect bony prominences
options.rationale: The client cannot feel pressure, so scheduled turning and skin checks prevent pressure injuries.

options.text: Massage reddened areas over bony prominences
options.rationale: Massaging reddened areas damages fragile tissue and is not recommended. Pressure should be relieved instead.

options.text: Perform passive range-of-motion exercises to all extremities
options.rationale: ROM prevents contractures and supports circulation in paralyzed limbs.

options.text: Teach weight shifts every 15-30 minutes when sitting in a wheelchair
options.rationale: Sitting concentrates pressure on the ischial tuberosities. Frequent pressure relief prevents breakdown.

options.text: Measure calf circumference only if the client reports leg pain
options.rationale: The client cannot feel leg pain below the injury. DVT must be watched for with routine assessment of swelling, warmth, and calf or thigh measurements.

questions.explanation: SCI complications include DVT and PE, pressure injuries, contractures, pneumonia, UTI, and autonomic dysreflexia. Because sensation is absent, the nurse cannot rely on client reports and must use scheduled assessments, turning, pressure relief, ROM, and DVT prophylaxis.

questions.stem: Two weeks after a C7 spinal cord injury, a 22-year-old client refuses physical therapy and says, "What's the point? My life is over." Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "You need to go to therapy if you want to get better."
options.rationale: This dismisses the client's feelings and may increase resistance. It does not address the client's grief.

options.text: "This is a huge loss. Tell me more about what you're feeling right now."
options.rationale: Acknowledging the loss and inviting the client to talk is therapeutic. It supports the grieving process and allows assessment for depression and suicide risk.

options.text: "Lots of people have it much worse than you do."
options.rationale: Comparing the client to others minimizes their feelings and closes off communication.

options.text: "Don't worry, with enough therapy you'll be walking again soon."
options.rationale: This gives false reassurance. No one can promise a return to walking after a cervical cord injury, and unrealistic promises damage trust.

questions.explanation: Clients with SCI often go through grief stages, including denial, anger, and depression. The nurse uses therapeutic communication, screens for depression and suicide risk, involves the family, and connects the client with counseling, peer support, and the rehab team. Setting realistic goals and building independence (adaptive equipment, home modification) support adjustment and successful home care.
